catalog_quote: [p.115] Stress, tone, duration, and intonation are not equally important in every language. English, for example, uses stress for semantic differentiation, as evidenced in the contrasts ab'stract (verb) v. 'abstract (noun), and re'call (verb) v. 'recall (noun). French and Mbili use it for emphasis. Duration is a distinctive feature in English, but not in French or Mbili. Mbili uses tone for semantic contrast, while neither English nor French use it at all. [p.116] Kreidler's definition of suprasegmental phonology conspicuously leaves out phonemic pitch or tone. Our discussion of suprasegmentals in Mbili focuses almost exclusively on tones - the language's primary distinctive suprasegmental feature. new_statements.rule_in_words: Mbili is described as a tone language (H, L, plus phonemic/derived M; CVCV stems H/HL/LH/LL; floating tones, downstep). Stress is explicitly said NOT to be used for lexical/semantic differentiation in Mbili -- only 'for emphasis' -- and the author adopts Clements & Goldsmith's definition of a tone language 'in which accent plays no lexical role' (p.138). No rule for the position of word stress is given anywhere in the grammar (the index lists every page treating stress: 115-117, 182, 297, all checked).
new_statements.exceptions: None; p.297 'paradigmatic stress or focus' refers to a declarative/focus marker ləgə, i.e. morphosyntactic emphasis, not phonological stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Stress/duration/intonation are treated (p.182) as applying 'to syntactic units such as the sentence', i.e. emphatic/phrase-level use only; tone is the word-level prosodic system.
new_statements.identity_note: Ayuninjam describes 'Mbili' = the Bambili (Mbeligi/Mbəlīgi) variety of Glottolog's Bambili-Bambui [bamb1266], ISO baw; the Bambui (Mbui) variety is not separately described. Same language as the target; no separate dialect glottocode needed.
